# Sleemi Law — Law Offices of Usmaan Sleemi

> New Jersey employment law firm representing individuals and small-to-mid-sized businesses in all employment matters. Office: 66 NJ-17, Suite 500, Paramus, NJ 07652. Phone: (973) 866-9415. Free, confidential consultations.

Sleemi Law (the Law Offices of Usmaan Sleemi) is a New Jersey employment law firm based in Paramus, New Jersey, representing individual employees and small-to-mid-sized businesses. Founding attorney Usmaan Sleemi was named a Super Lawyers Rising Star in 2019 and 2020 and a Top Lawyer by Morris/Essex Health & Life Magazine in 2018. The firm handles wrongful termination, employment discrimination, sexual harassment, hostile work environment, retaliation, whistleblower (CEPA), wage and hour/unpaid wages, equal pay, family and medical leave (FMLA/NJFLA), severance review and negotiation, employment contract and non-compete negotiation, disability accommodation, pregnancy accommodation, and religious accommodation matters. Strict statutes of limitations apply to New Jersey employment claims (generally two years under the NJLAD, one year under CEPA).

## Practice areas
- [Wrongful Termination](https://www.sleemilaw.com/wrongful-termination/): Wrongful termination in New Jersey means being fired for an illegal reason — such as discrimination, retaliation, or refusal to break the law — and employees generally have two years from the termination date to sue under the NJ Law Against Discrimination or CEPA.
- [Employment Discrimination](https://www.sleemilaw.com/employment-discrimination/): Employment discrimination in New Jersey is treating an employee or applicant worse because of a protected characteristic — race, religion, sex, gender identity or expression, age, disability, national origin, sexual orientation, pregnancy, marital status, or ancestry — and it is illegal under the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (NJLAD).
- [Sexual Harassment](https://www.sleemilaw.com/sexual-harassment/): Sexual harassment in New Jersey is any unwelcome sexual advance, request for sexual favors, or verbal or physical sexual conduct that affects employment decisions or creates a hostile work environment, and it is illegal under the NJLAD and Title VII.
- [Hostile Work Environment](https://www.sleemilaw.com/hostile-work-environment/): A hostile work environment exists under New Jersey law when severe or pervasive mistreatment based on a protected characteristic — harassment, slurs, intimidation, or humiliation — makes a reasonable person's working conditions intolerable, and employers can be liable even if HR was never told.
- [Retaliation](https://www.sleemilaw.com/retaliation/): Retaliation in New Jersey is any adverse action — termination, demotion, schedule or pay cuts, exclusion, or hostile treatment — taken because an employee engaged in protected activity such as complaining about discrimination or reporting illegal conduct, and it is illegal under the NJLAD and CEPA.
- [Whistleblower (CEPA)](https://www.sleemilaw.com/whistleblower/): New Jersey's Conscientious Employee Protection Act (CEPA) protects employees who disclose, object to, or refuse to participate in illegal or fraudulent employer activity, and it is considered the strongest whistleblower statute in the country.
- [Wage and Hour Disputes / Unpaid Wages](https://www.sleemilaw.com/wage-and-hour-disputes/): New Jersey employees are owed one-and-a-half times their regular rate for hours over 40 per week under both state and federal law, and employers who fail to pay wages, overtime, commissions, or final paychecks on time face liquidated damages that can double the amount owed.
- [Equal Pay](https://www.sleemilaw.com/equal-pay/): The Diane B. Allen Equal Pay Act — part of the NJLAD — prohibits paying an employee less than a colleague for substantially similar work because of any protected characteristic, and it allows recovery of up to six years of back pay plus treble damages.
- [Family and Medical Leave (FMLA)](https://www.sleemilaw.com/family-medical-leave-fmla/): The federal Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) and the New Jersey Family Leave Act (NJFLA) give eligible employees protected, unpaid, job-protected leave for their own or a family member's serious health condition and for bonding with a new child, with reinstatement rights when the leave ends.
- [Severance Review / Negotiation](https://www.sleemilaw.com/severance-review/): A severance agreement in New Jersey is a contract: the employee receives money or benefits and, in exchange, signs away the right to sue the employer — so every severance offer should be reviewed by an attorney before signing, especially the release of claims and any non-disparagement or cooperation clauses.
- [Employment Contract Negotiation](https://www.sleemilaw.com/employment-contract-negotiation/): Restrictive covenants such as non-compete agreements are enforceable in New Jersey only to the extent they protect the employer's legitimate interests and are reasonable in duration, geographic reach, and scope of activity — a standard that lets courts narrow or strike overreaching agreements.
- [Disability Accommodation](https://www.sleemilaw.com/disability-accommodation/): Under the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination and the federal ADA, New Jersey employers must provide reasonable accommodations — modified duties, schedule changes, equipment, or leave — that let a qualified employee with a disability perform the job, unless doing so would impose an undue hardship.
- [Pregnancy Accommodation](https://www.sleemilaw.com/pregnancy-accommodation/): The New Jersey Pregnant Worker Fairness Act and the NJLAD require employers to provide reasonable accommodations — lighter duty, more frequent breaks, schedule changes, or modified equipment — for pregnancy, childbirth, and related medical conditions, and prohibit forcing an employee onto leave when an accommodation would let her keep working.
- [Religious Accommodation](https://www.sleemilaw.com/religious-accommodation/): New Jersey employers must reasonably accommodate an employee's sincerely held religious beliefs and practices — including scheduling around Sabbath or holiday observance, prayer breaks, and religious dress or grooming — unless the accommodation would cause an undue hardship on business operations.

## Q&A resources
- [Can My Employer Fire Me for No Reason in New Jersey?](https://www.sleemilaw.com/blog/can-employer-fire-you-for-no-reason-new-jersey/): Yes — New Jersey is an at-will employment state, so an employer can generally fire an employee at any time, with or without a reason. The exception: a termination is illegal if it is based on discrimination, retaliation, breach of an employment contract, or a violation of public policy.
- [How Long Do I Have to File a Wrongful Termination Claim in New Jersey?](https://www.sleemilaw.com/blog/time-limit-file-wrongful-termination-claim-nj/): Most wrongful termination claims in New Jersey — including NJLAD discrimination claims and CEPA whistleblower claims — must be filed within two years of the termination. CEPA whistleblower claims move faster than people expect, and some contract claims have shorter deadlines written into the agreement.
- [What Should I Do If I'm Being Sexually Harassed at Work in New Jersey?](https://www.sleemilaw.com/blog/what-to-do-sexual-harassment-at-work-new-jersey/): If you are being sexually harassed at work in New Jersey: (1) tell the harasser to stop if it is safe to do so, (2) preserve every text, email, and message, (3) report the conduct in writing to HR or management, and (4) talk to an employment lawyer before quitting or signing anything. Reporting harassment is protected activity — retaliation for it is illegal.
- [Is My Employer Required to Pay Me Overtime in New Jersey?](https://www.sleemilaw.com/blog/overtime-pay-rules-new-jersey/): Yes — New Jersey employees who work more than 40 hours in a workweek must be paid one-and-a-half times their regular rate of pay, unless they fall under a specific exemption such as the executive, administrative, or professional exemptions. Paying a salary does not automatically exempt an employee from overtime.
- [Should You Sign the Severance Agreement Your Employer Offered You?](https://www.sleemilaw.com/blog/should-you-sign-severance-agreement-nj/): Not before an attorney reviews it. A severance agreement is a contract in which you receive money in exchange for waiving your right to sue. Once signed, the waiver usually extinguishes discrimination, wage, and whistleblower claims. Employees 40 and over must receive at least 21 days to consider and 7 days to revoke a release of age discrimination claims.
- [What Is the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (NJLAD)?](https://www.sleemilaw.com/blog/new-jersey-law-against-discrimination-explained/): The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (NJLAD) is New Jersey's principal anti-discrimination statute. It prohibits discrimination based on race, religion, sex, gender identity, pregnancy, sexual orientation, age, disability, national origin, and other protected characteristics — and it applies to nearly all NJ employers, with no cap on compensatory or punitive damages.
- [Can My Employer Retaliate Against Me for Reporting Discrimination in New Jersey?](https://www.sleemilaw.com/blog/employer-retaliation-reporting-discrimination-nj/): No. Under the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination, it is illegal for an employer to retaliate against an employee for reporting discrimination, participating in an investigation, or requesting an accommodation. Retaliation is a separate violation even if the underlying discrimination claim is not proven — and timing is the key evidence.
- [Are Non-Competes Enforceable in New Jersey?](https://www.sleemilaw.com/blog/are-non-competes-enforceable-new-jersey/): Yes — non-compete agreements are enforceable in New Jersey, but only if they protect the employer's legitimate business interests and are reasonable in duration, geographic scope, and the activities they restrict. New Jersey courts can narrow overbroad agreements rather than void them entirely, so the exact wording matters enormously.
